digest.definition: The study of how people shape and are shaped by their social world and their relations with others, drawing on evidence to inform action on social issues from local to global
distinctiveFeatures: The study of how people shape and are shaped by their social world and their relations with others, drawing on evidence to inform action on social issues from local to global
A core social science that joins theory and evidence, so that students learn to apply and test both theories and methods
Explains inequality through social structures and drivers rather than individual choice; questions of equity, diversity and inclusion are central to it
Ranges across time, place and scale, from macro structures to face-to-face interaction, and uses quantitative, qualitative, mixed and creative methods
Three interlinked purposes, academic, vocational and professional, which feed one another
Reflexive about its own canon: it asks students to question historically dominant theories, to look beyond European founding figures and to consider colonial legacies
Has no accrediting body; works with professional associations

themesInSubject.inThisSubject: central to the discipline, which studies stratification and unequal access to wealth and power and their intersections; expected in every curriculum, with safe handling of contested topics and equal respect in all settings (D1, 1.6 to 1.8)

designed in from admission to assessment so that adjustments are rarely needed; digital access, accessible rooms and language that does not make disabled people the object of study (D1, 1.9 to 1.12, 3.14, 3.21)

a critical lens on environmental integrity, social justice and prosperity, with a critique of the SDGs as well as engagement with them; ESD through teaching and assessment, not content alone (D1, 1.13 to 1.18)
widening theory beyond European founders, critiquing Western knowledge, routes through guests, mobility, Global South partners, students' own backgrounds and online collaboration (D1, 1.19 to 1.26)

named employability, entrepreneurship and enterprise education; the subject's research and critical skills as employability, delivered with careers services and outside partners (D1, 1.27 to 1.34, 3.19)

AI treated as both a tool and a social reality to study critically (power, bias, environmental cost, authorship); critical use in teaching and assessment within institutional policy; one transferable skill (D1, 1.35 to 1.41, 3.10, 3.15, 4.5)

subjectSpecific.text: You should be able to explain how colonial histories still shape the world today, and why some knowledge and viewpoints are valued more than others.

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: equality, diversity and inclusion built into every curriculum
statements.paraphrase: Equity, diversity and inclusion are central to the subject, which explains inequality through social drivers and structures rather than individual choices; every Sociology course is expected to build questions of equality, diversity and inclusion into its curriculum.

forPractitioner.text: Make equality, diversity and inclusion part of the curriculum itself, not an add-on: the subject reads inequality as structural, and the statement expects this of every course.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: an expectation of the course; the student meets its effect in what is taught

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.appliesTo: institutions and everyone involved in a course
statements.about: fair treatment under equality law; inclusion through the student journey
statements.paraphrase: Equality, diversity and inclusion shape how Sociology curricula are designed and run; the law requires institutions to make sure staff and students are treated fairly and not discriminated against, and inclusion should reach past the law into curriculum design, content, teaching, assessment and feedback.

forPractitioner.text: Treat the legal duty of fair, non-discriminatory treatment as the floor and go past it: consider the diversity of your students in curriculum design, content, teaching, assessment and feedback so that every student can succeed.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a legal duty on the institution, reported by the statement

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: safe study of contested topics; inclusive curricula; respect in every setting
statements.paraphrase: Students meet difficult and contested topics, and should be supported to argue from evidence and engage with differing views in a safe, inclusive setting while reflecting on their own; curricula should be made more inclusive so students question historically dominant theories, courses should be inclusive for all, and course teams should, where they can, see that every student is equally respected on campus, on trips and on placement.

forPractitioner.text: Support students to handle contested topics with evidence in a safe, inclusive space; keep resources accessible and responsive; widen the curriculum so students question theories that have dominated; and, wherever possible, make sure every student is treated with equal respect in every setting the course uses.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a set of duties on the course team and institution

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: accessibility designed in from the start
statements.paraphrase: Courses commit to accessibility in the widest sense; course design should include accessibility from the start, and delivery should make teaching, assessment, activities and fieldtrips accessible without students having to ask for individual adjustments.

forPractitioner.text: Design accessibility in from the outset so that teaching, assessment, activities and fieldtrips work for disabled students without each having to request an adjustment.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course design and delivery

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: flexible, accessible courses with adjustments in the design
statements.paraphrase: Courses should be flexible and accessible, in admissions, resources, fieldwork, fieldtrips and teamwork, and should build accessibility and inclusive practice in so that disabled students are not singled out and adjustments are part of the course design.

forPractitioner.text: Make the course flexible and accessible across admissions, resources, fieldwork and group work, with adjustments built into the design so no disabled student is singled out.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree
Accessibility and the needs of disabled students

statements.about: digital and physical access; inclusive language about disability
statements.paraphrase: Once students are enrolled, digital accessibility matters, above all in blended learning; classrooms and study spaces should be accessible to all, language and approaches should not cast disabled people as other or as objects of study, and research and teaching that explore disabled people's lived experience are valued.

forPractitioner.text: Keep materials digitally accessible, make rooms and study spaces accessible, use language that does not treat disabled people as the object of study, and value approaches that draw on their lived experience.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the course and its spaces

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: education for sustainable development across curriculum, teaching and assessment
statements.paraphrase: Education for sustainable development should underpin teaching, learning and assessment as well as the curriculum; the QAA and Advance HE guidance's three ways (thinking, practising, being) may help, and its interdisciplinary nature suits co-created, problem-based work with students, tutors and partners on real challenges.

forPractitioner.text: Let education for sustainable development shape how you teach and assess, not only what you teach; the three-fold frame of the national ESD guidance can help, as can co-created, problem-based projects with outside partners.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on curriculum, teaching and assessment design

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: international guest lecturers
statements.paraphrase: Internationalisation should be pursued through teaching as well as the curriculum, one route being lectures from international guests.

forPractitioner.text: Bring in guest lecturers from other countries as one way of internationalising teaching.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a route the course should take; not a student standard

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: student mobility: trips, study abroad, placements
statements.paraphrase: One route is promoting student mobility, through field trips, study abroad and placements overseas.

forPractitioner.text: Promote student mobility, such as field trips, a period of study abroad or an international placement.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a route the course should take; not a student standard

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: collaboration with Global South institutions
statements.paraphrase: One route is exploring partnerships with institutions in the Global South so students meet other sociological standpoints in a meaningful way.

forPractitioner.text: Explore partnerships with institutions in the Global South to give students real engagement with other sociological standpoints.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a route the course should take; not a student standard

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: students' cultural backgrounds as standpoints
statements.paraphrase: One route is celebrating the cultural backgrounds students bring as sources of other sociological standpoints.

forPractitioner.text: Treat the varied cultural backgrounds of your students as a resource for alternative sociological standpoints.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a route the course should take; not a student standard

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: Collaborative Online International Learning
statements.paraphrase: One route is promoting Collaborative Online International Learning.

forPractitioner.text: Promote Collaborative Online International Learning (shared online work with students in other countries).

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a route the course should take; not a student standard

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: teaching that values what students bring
statements.paraphrase: Internationalisation needs teaching that values the distinct knowledge students bring with them, for example through dialogue that helps students see themselves as legitimate contributors to knowledge.

forPractitioner.text: If you aim to internationalise, teach in a way that values what students already know, for instance through dialogue that lets them see themselves as rightful contributors to knowledge.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a condition on teaching practice

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.about: working with careers services and employers on EEE education
statements.paraphrase: Course teams should work with careers services, partnership staff, alumni, social enterprises and employers to design and deliver employability, enterprise and entrepreneurship education and to open pathways for students, for example through visiting lectures, master classes and client briefs with scaffolded career tasks.

forPractitioner.text: Work with careers staff, alumni, social enterprises and employers to plan and deliver EEE education, using visiting speakers, master classes or client briefs with career tasks built around them.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on course teams

headingPath: Context and purposes of a Sociology degree

statements.appliesTo: students and those who teach them
statements.about: critical engagement with generative AI
statements.paraphrase: Teaching can use generative AI to build digital literacy while keeping to the subject's core questions, and students should be encouraged to approach new tools critically, weighing what they make possible against what is lost when they stand in for human dialogue and creativity, so that the voices of marginalised people are kept.

forPractitioner.text: Encourage students to use AI tools critically: what they make easier, and what goes missing when human talk and creativity are handed over, including the risk of erasing marginalised voices.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be encouraged to use new AI tools critically, asking both what they help you do and what is lost when they replace human dialogue and creativity, including whose voices go missing.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Sociology degree

statements.about: skills to examine structure and agency; social phenomena across levels
statements.paraphrase: Courses give an education in the theory, methods, analysis and practice of the subject; students are expected to build skills to examine how institutions and structures mould human agency and are moulded by it, and to understand social life at the global, community and personal scales and the links between them.

forPractitioner.text: Design the course so students build the skills to analyse how institutions and structures mould human agency and are moulded by it, and to connect global, community and personal levels of social life; the statement expects this of students.

forBeneficiary.text: You are expected to build the skills to examine how social structures and institutions shape people's actions and are shaped by them, and to understand social life from the global to the personal and how these levels link.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Sociology degree

statements.appliesTo: graduates and students after a programme of study
statements.about: the distinctiveness of the subject and its shared concerns
statements.paraphrase: The subject gives tools used across the social sciences and is often studied with other subjects; once their studies end, students and graduates should be able to understand and value what makes Sociology distinct (its standpoints, explanations, levels of analysis, use of theory and evidence) and what it shares with other disciplines.

forPractitioner.text: By the end of the programme, students should be able to say what makes Sociology distinct, in standpoint, explanation, levels of analysis, theory and evidence, and where it overlaps with neighbouring subjects.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your studies you should be able to explain what makes Sociology different from neighbouring subjects, in how it explains, the levels it works at and how it uses theory and evidence, and what it has in common with them.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Sociology degree

statements.appliesTo: undergraduates on joint or combined Sociology courses
statements.about: core skills in joint and combined honours
statements.paraphrase: Undergraduates taking Sociology in a joint or combined degree, including major and minor routes, will reach core parts of the subject-specific and generic skills set out here and will add others from their other subject, and may explore the overlaps.

forPractitioner.text: Joint and combined honours students will achieve the core of the statement's subject and generic skills, not necessarily all of them, and will add skills from their other subject.

forBeneficiary.text: If you study Sociology alongside another subject, you will gain the core of its subject and general skills and add skills from your other subject, with room to explore where the two overlap.

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Sociology degree

statements.about: varied, flexible teaching for diverse learning needs
statements.paraphrase: Teaching and assessment vary between departments, but every Sociology course is expected to value varied, flexible teaching and learning styles that reflect students' diverse needs, so students meet many kinds of teaching and assessment.

forPractitioner.text: Use a range of flexible teaching, learning and assessment styles that reflect the varied needs of your students; the statement expects this of every course whatever its orientation.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: an expectation of courses

headingPath: Distinctive features of a Sociology degree

statements.about: external reviewers in periodic review
statements.paraphrase: Externality is essential to UK quality assurance; providers will use external reviewers in periodic review for an independent view on changes and to make sure threshold standards are met and content suits the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Include external reviewers in periodic review to get an independent view of proposed changes and to confirm that threshold standards are met and content fits the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a provider duty in quality assurance

statements.about: scaffolded experimentation with theory across the levels
statements.paraphrase: Teaching supports students in experimenting with theory, and this should be scaffolded and returned to at each level of study.

forPractitioner.text: Give students room to try out theory, and scaffold and revisit that work at every level of the course.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the design of teaching

statements.about: colonial legacies and whose knowledge is valued
statements.paraphrase: Decolonisation draws on knowledge, research and theory from across the world and helps students see that some knowledge and perspectives are valued above others; students should be able to explain how colonial legacies matter today.

forPractitioner.text: Draw on knowledge and theory from across the world so students see how some perspectives are valued above others; students should be able to explain the effects of colonial legacies now.

forBeneficiary.text: You should be able to explain how colonial histories still shape the world today, and why some knowledge and viewpoints are valued more than others.

statements.about: explaining assessment of and for learning
statements.paraphrase: Assessment matters as students progress; the difference between assessing what has been learned and assessing to support learning, and the value of each, should be explained clearly to students.

forPractitioner.text: Explain clearly to students how assessment of learning differs from assessment for learning and why both matter.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on staff to explain; the student receives it

statements.about: equitable, accessible assessment, reviewed regularly
statements.paraphrase: Since assessment can reproduce inequality, it matters that assessments take account of equality and diversity and are accessible and inclusive, reducing later adjustments; offering choice can widen access, and assessments should be reviewed regularly to stay fit for purpose.

forPractitioner.text: Design assessment with equality and diversity in mind so it is accessible from the start, consider giving students a choice of approach, and review assessments regularly.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on assessment design

statements.about: varied assessment; knowing local policy on technology
statements.paraphrase: Many inclusive forms of assessment suit the subject, from posters and autoethnography to essays and exams, and digital forms are growing; staff and students should know their institution's policies on technology in teaching and assessment, and generative AI offers scope for imaginative tasks.

forPractitioner.text: Use a wide range of inclusive assessment forms, including digital ones, and make sure staff and students know the institution's policies on technology in teaching and assessment.

forBeneficiary.text: You should know your institution's rules on using technology, including AI tools, in your learning and assessment, and expect to be assessed in many forms, from posters and podcasts to essays and exams.

statements.about: transparent assessment and clear rubrics
statements.paraphrase: Assessment should be transparent and clearly communicated so students know how and why they are assessed; clear rubrics are called essential.

forPractitioner.text: Tell students how and why they will be assessed and give them clear rubrics; the statement calls these essential.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on assessment practice

statements.about: evidence above threshold; Annex D for classifications
statements.paraphrase: Most students will do much better than the threshold; each provider decides what evidence shows this and should refer to Annex D of the qualification frameworks, which describes the four honours classifications.

forPractitioner.text: Use your own method for judging achievement above the threshold, and refer to Annex D of the UK qualification frameworks, which describes first, upper second, lower second and third class honours.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider in classifying degrees

statements.about: threshold standards are not competence standards; EHRC guidance
statements.paraphrase: The threshold standards are not meant as universal competence standards; a provider that sets competence standards under the Equality Act 2010 in a programme specification may draw on this statement and any professional body requirements, and should then follow the latest Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance.

forPractitioner.text: Do not treat the threshold lists as competence standards; if you set competence standards in a programme specification, draw on the statement if useful and follow the Equality and Human Rights Commission's current guidance.

forBeneficiary.text: not-applicable: a duty on the provider

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: key concepts and theoretical approaches
statements.paraphrase: Can set out and look closely at a range of the subject's central concepts and theoretical approaches.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to set out and examine a range of central concepts and theoretical approaches.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to explain and look critically at a range of the main ideas and theories in Sociology.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: how Sociology differs from other ways of explaining
statements.paraphrase: Can say what sets sociological understanding and explanation apart from other kinds.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to explain what distinguishes sociological explanation from other ways of understanding the social world.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to explain what makes a sociological explanation different from other ways of making sense of the world.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: discussing topics with theory and evidence, in varied formats
statements.paraphrase: Can discuss sociological topics drawing on theory and evidence, take part in current debates and present conclusions in different formats.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to discuss sociological topics with theory and evidence, engage with current debates and present conclusions in several formats.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to discuss sociological topics using theory and evidence, join current debates and present your conclusions in different formats.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: processes of social change, conflict and stability
statements.paraphrase: Can explain the processes behind social change, conflict and stability.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to explain the processes beneath social change, conflict and stability.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to explain what drives social change and conflict, and what keeps societies stable.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: individuals, groups, structures and the environment
statements.paraphrase: Can describe how individuals, groups and social structures relate to one another and to the natural and physical environment.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to describe how individuals, groups and social structures relate to each other and to the natural and physical environment.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to describe how people, groups and social structures relate to one another and to the natural and built world.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: power, colonial legacies, inequity and injustice
statements.paraphrase: Can show awareness of how power imbalances, colonial legacies, inequity and injustice are bound up with one another.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to show awareness of how power imbalances, colonial legacies, inequities and injustices connect.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to show you are aware of how unequal power, colonial histories and injustice are linked.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: specialist knowledge used to build an argument
statements.paraphrase: Can draw on specialist knowledge of at least one area within the subject to build a sociological argument.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to use specialist knowledge of one or more sub-areas to construct a sociological argument.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to use your specialist knowledge of at least one area of Sociology to build an argument.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: comparison across time or context
statements.paraphrase: Can judge how comparison is used in the subject, whether across time or across settings.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to evaluate the use of comparison, over time (diachronic) or across contexts (synchronic).

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to judge how well comparison works in Sociology, whether you compare across time or across places.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: perspectives on diversity, inequality and power
statements.paraphrase: Can understand the different sociological perspectives on social diversity and inequality, taking in the main dimensions and sites of power.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to understand the range of sociological perspectives on diversity and inequality and address the main dimensions and sites of power.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should understand the different sociological views of diversity and inequality and the main places where power operates.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: analysing data on social inequality
statements.paraphrase: Can analyse quantitative and qualitative data to grasp patterns of social inequality, what drives concern about them and what follows from them.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to analyse quantitative and qualitative data to understand patterns in social inequalities and their consequences.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to analyse numbers and qualitative material to find patterns of inequality and what they lead to.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: global and local social problems; interdisciplinary approaches
statements.paraphrase: Can assess complex social problems at global and local scale and the forces shaping them, and help bring several disciplines to bear on them. The item's wording runs two clauses together (Part E).

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to judge complex social problems, global and local, and the forces at work, and contribute to multi- and interdisciplinary approaches.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to assess complex social problems, local and global, and the forces behind them, and help other subjects work on them with you.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: summarising research and critiquing its frameworks and methods
statements.paraphrase: Can summarise and explain what empirical sociological research has found, and critically assess the frameworks, theories and methods it used.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to summarise and explain empirical findings and give a critical assessment of the frameworks, theories and methods behind them.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to sum up and explain what sociological research has found, and judge critically the theories and methods it used.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: choosing research strategies and methods
statements.paraphrase: Can judge how suitable a range of research strategies and methods are for identifying social problems.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to evaluate how well a range of research strategies and methods suit the identification of social problems.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to judge which research approaches and methods suit the social problem you want to study.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: using qualitative and quantitative methodologies in design
statements.paraphrase: Can use both qualitative and quantitative methodologies in framing and designing research.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to draw on qualitative and quantitative methodologies when framing problems and designing research.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to use both qualitative and quantitative approaches when you frame and design research.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: research tools, software and basic statistics
statements.paraphrase: Can use suitable tools to collect and analyse both numerical and qualitative data, with software and with basic statistical and interpretive procedures.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to use suitable tools for gathering and analysing both kinds of data, including software and basic statistical and interpretive techniques.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to use the right tools to gather and analyse numerical and qualitative data, including software and basic statistics.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: ethics of social research in different settings
statements.paraphrase: Can analyse the ethical implications of social research across different research settings.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to analyse the ethical implications of social research in varied settings.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to work through the ethical questions social research raises in different settings.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: planning and completing an independent project
statements.paraphrase: Can plan and finish a Sociology project working independently.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to plan and complete a Sociology project on their own.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to plan and complete a Sociology project of your own.

headingPath: Threshold level: Subject knowledge, understanding and skills

statements.about: sociology applied to policy
statements.paraphrase: Can recognise how sociological knowledge bears on policy (social, public, civic and environmental), and the place and worth of the subject in policy.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to recognise how sociological knowledge is applied to social, public, civic and environmental policy and what the subject contributes there.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to see how sociological knowledge is used in social, public and environmental policy and why it matters there.

statements.about: scholarly work in a range of formats
statements.paraphrase: Can carry out and present scholarly work in different formats.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to undertake scholarly work and present it in several formats.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to carry out academic work and present it in different formats.

statements.about: weighing rival explanations; evidence-based responses
statements.paraphrase: Can weigh competing explanations and respond on the basis of evidence.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to assess rival explanations and give responses grounded in evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to weigh up competing explanations and respond using evidence.

statements.about: communicating in different contexts
statements.paraphrase: Can communicate with other people in a range of settings.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to communicate with others across varied contexts.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to communicate well with different people in different settings.

statements.about: digital skills for organising and presenting ideas
statements.paraphrase: Can use digital technology and skills to organise and present ideas.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to use digital technology and skills in organising and presenting ideas.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to use digital tools to organise your ideas and present them.

statements.about: retrieving and synthesising information
statements.paraphrase: Can show skill in finding information and drawing it together.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to demonstrate information retrieval and synthesis.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to find information and bring it together into a coherent whole.

statements.about: clear, reasoned discussion with others
statements.paraphrase: Can discuss and present ideas with other people clearly and with reasons.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to discuss and present ideas with others clearly and with reasoning.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to discuss and present ideas with others clearly and with good reasons.

statements.about: working alone and in groups
statements.paraphrase: Can show the ability to work both independently and in groups.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to demonstrate independent and group working.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to show you can work on your own and in a group.

statements.about: applying research principles ethically
statements.paraphrase: Can understand how to put research principles and practices into effect ethically.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should understand how to apply research principles and practices ethically.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should understand how to carry out research in an ethical way.

statements.about: using and evaluating AI and digital technology, including generative AI
statements.paraphrase: Can use artificial intelligence and other digital technologies, generative AI among them, appropriately, and evaluate their implications critically.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to use AI and other digital technologies appropriately, including generative AI, and critically evaluate what they imply.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to use AI and other digital tools, including generative AI, in suitable ways and judge critically what they mean for your work and for society.

statements.about: making knowledge and argument understandable
statements.paraphrase: Can present knowledge or an argument so that others can follow it.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to present knowledge or argument in a way others can understand.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to present what you know, or an argument, so that others can follow it.

statements.about: intellectual independence and critical judgement
statements.paraphrase: Can show intellectual independence: working on tasks alone with suitable support, carrying out self-directed research and exercising critical judgement.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to show intellectual independence, taking on tasks with suitable guidance, doing self-directed research and showing critical judgement.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to think and work independently, with the right support, carry out your own research and use critical judgement.

statements.about: computer-aided data storage and analysis
statements.paraphrase: Can use computer-based techniques to store, collate and analyse quantitative and qualitative data.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to use computer-based techniques for storing, collating and analysing both kinds of data.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to use computer tools to store, organise and analyse numerical and qualitative data.

statements.about: collaborative work in teams and discussion
statements.paraphrase: Can work collaboratively, in a group or team or by taking part in discussion.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to collaborate, working in a group or team or taking part in discussion.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to work with others, in a team or in discussion.

statements.about: values and ethics in culture, society and self
statements.paraphrase: Can identify and examine the values and ethics beneath culture and society and in one's own life.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to identify and examine underlying values and ethics, social and cultural as well as personal.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to identify and question the values and ethics behind culture, society and your own views.

statements.about: wellbeing, emotions and learning
statements.paraphrase: Can understand why wellbeing, mental health and emotions matter and how they bear on learning.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should understand why wellbeing, mental health and emotions matter and how they bear on learning.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should understand why your wellbeing, mental health and emotions matter and how they affect your learning.

statements.about: using feedback for development
statements.paraphrase: Can make good use of feedback to further intellectual development.

forPractitioner.text: At threshold, honours graduates should be able to use feedback appropriately to develop intellectually.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your degree you should be able to use the feedback you receive to keep developing your thinking.

statements.about: synthesising theory, concepts and empirical research on current problems
statements.paraphrase: Should bring theoretical, conceptual and empirical research together when discussing present-day social problems.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to synthesise theory, concepts and empirical research when they discuss contemporary social problems.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to bring theory, concepts and research findings together when you discuss current social problems.

statements.about: critical awareness of the contexts and theories behind the subject
statements.paraphrase: Should show critical awareness of the theories, and the historical, cultural, social, political and environmental settings, that shape the subject.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to show critical awareness of the historical, cultural, social, political and environmental settings and theories that shape the discipline.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be critically aware of the historical, cultural, political and environmental settings and theories that shape Sociology.

statements.about: critical discussion of power, colonial legacies and injustice
statements.paraphrase: Should discuss critically how power imbalance, colonial legacies, inequity and injustice connect and overlap.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to discuss critically the connections and overlaps between power imbalance, colonial legacies, inequity and injustice.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to discuss critically how unequal power, colonial histories and injustice connect and overlap.

statements.about: designing and carrying out research with both kinds of source
statements.paraphrase: Should design and conduct sociological research drawing on quantitative and qualitative sources.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to design and conduct sociological research using quantitative and qualitative sources.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to design and carry out sociological research using both numerical and qualitative sources.

statements.about: assessing methodologies for complex problems
statements.paraphrase: Should critically judge which methodologies suit complex problems.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to critically assess suitable methodologies for complex problems.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to judge critically which research methodologies suit complex problems.

statements.about: sensitive and ethical issues in research
statements.paraphrase: Should discuss the sensitive and ethical questions that sociological research raises.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to discuss sensitive and ethical issues in sociological research.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to discuss the sensitive and ethical questions that come up in sociological research.

statements.about: selecting and using research tools, software and statistics
statements.paraphrase: Should choose and use suitable tools to gather or analyse quantitative and qualitative data, with software and basic statistical and interpretive procedures.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to select and use suitable tools to collect and/or analyse both kinds of data, including software and basic statistical and interpretive procedures.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to choose and use the right tools, software and basic statistics to gather or analyse numerical and qualitative data.

statements.about: complex concepts; independent work with some originality
statements.paraphrase: Should discuss and analyse complex concepts critically and work independently with a degree of originality. The item joins a subject skill and a generic one (Part E).

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to discuss and analyse complex concepts critically and work on their own with some originality.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to discuss and analyse complex ideas critically and work on your own with some originality.

statements.about: completing a research project with original or reworked data
statements.paraphrase: Should complete a research project that generates or reformulates data and rests on a critical understanding of the subject. The item reads 'generation of reformulation', most likely a slip for 'or' (Part E).

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to complete a research project that generates or reformulates data, informed by a critical understanding of the subject.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to complete a research project in which you produce or rework data, guided by a critical understanding of Sociology.

statements.about: evaluating policies and interventions with theory and evidence
statements.paraphrase: Should evaluate social policies and interventions critically, using social theory, frameworks and evidence.

forPractitioner.text: Master's graduates should be able to critically evaluate social policies and interventions using social theories, frameworks and evidence.

forBeneficiary.text: By the end of your master's you should be able to judge social policies and interventions critically using social theory, frameworks and evidence.
